[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_004] Prompt injection remains the top agent security risk
Security reviews continue to rank indirect prompt injection as the highest-impact risk for tool-using agents: untrusted documents or web pages carry instructions that attempt to redirect the agent, exfiltrate data or trigger destructive tool calls. Effective mitigations combine input provenance tagging, instruction/data separation in prompts, least-privilege tool permissions, per-task call budgets and human approval for irreversible actions. Detection alone is considered insufficient because attackers can paraphrase past filters.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_004] Prompt injection remains the top agent security risk
Security reviews continue to rank indirect prompt injection as the highest-impact risk for tool-using agents: untrusted documents or web pages carry instructions that attempt to redirect the agent, exfiltrate data or trigger destructive tool calls. Effective mitigations combine input provenance tagging, instruction/data separation in prompts, least-privilege tool permissions, per-task call budgets and human approval for irreversible actions. Detection alone is considered insufficient because attackers can paraphrase past filters.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_004] Prompt injection remains the top agent security risk
Security reviews continue to rank indirect prompt injection as the highest-impact risk for tool-using agents: untrusted documents or web pages carry instructions that attempt to redirect the agent, exfiltrate data or trigger destructive tool calls. Effective mitigations combine input provenance tagging, instruction/data separation in prompts, least-privilege tool permissions, per-task call budgets and human approval for irreversible actions. Detection alone is considered insufficient because attackers can paraphrase past filters.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_004] Prompt injection remains the top agent security risk
Security reviews continue to rank indirect prompt injection as the highest-impact risk for tool-using agents: untrusted documents or web pages carry instructions that attempt to redirect the agent, exfiltrate data or trigger destructive tool calls. Effective mitigations combine input provenance tagging, instruction/data separation in prompts, least-privilege tool permissions, per-task call budgets and human approval for irreversible actions. Detection alone is considered insufficient because attackers can paraphrase past filters.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_002] MCP adoption: from protocol proposal to enterprise tool gateway
Model Context Protocol servers are increasingly deployed as internal tool gateways: one MCP server fronts several internal systems, applies authentication, rate limits and audit logging, and exposes a curated tool list to all agent clients. This pattern centralizes permission policy in the gateway instead of duplicating it in every agent. Reviewers caution that exposing a large tool list degrades tool-selection accuracy, so gateways usually publish narrow, task-oriented tools rather than raw API passthroughs.

[web:web_006] Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

[web:web_009] When not to use multi-agent orchestration
Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.

[web:web_008] Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

[web:web_007] Observability requirements for production agent workflows
Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

[web:web_002] MCP adoption: from protocol proposal to enterprise tool gateway
Model Context Protocol servers are increasingly deployed as internal tool gateways: one MCP server fronts several internal systems, applies authentication, rate limits and audit logging, and exposes a curated tool list to all agent clients. This pattern centralizes permission policy in the gateway instead of duplicating it in every agent. Reviewers caution that exposing a large tool list degrades tool-selection accuracy, so gateways usually publish narrow, task-oriented tools rather than raw API passthroughs.
